covers.quote: Use initial capitals for commercial terms
An exception to using initial capitals is where the business itself uses an unusual mix of spacing, capitals and lower case letters. In this case, write it the way the business writes it.
Don’t use an initial capital at the start of sentences when the trade mark or brand starts with a lower case letter.
Use initial capitals for the proprietary names of drugs and other chemicals
use a capital letter.

rules.quote: Use initial capitals for trade marks, brands and business names.
rules.violation_condition: A trade mark, brand, business name or proprietary drug or chemical name is written with incorrect capitalisation, or an owner's unusual spacing and letter case is altered, including capitalising a normally lower-case brand initial at the start of a sentence.
when: The term identifies a trade mark, brand, business or proprietary drug or chemical.
Where the business uses unusual spacing or capitalisation, its own form takes precedence over ordinary initial capitals.
A brand's initial lower case letter stays lower case at the start of a sentence.
Generic names are covered by the separate lower-case rule.
rules.why: G-2 keeps owner-specific styling and sentence-position cases together; G-4 absorbs repeated proprietary-name capitalisation instructions without duplicating the separate brand-reference restriction.

covers.quote: Other brand names have become so widely used that they are no longer associated with a specific product. They have become common household names used in a generic sense. They start with lower case except at the start of a sentence.
A few words have different meanings when used as a trade mark or used generically.

rules.violation_condition: A generic drug or chemical name, or a former brand name used as an established generic word, has an inappropriate capital letter away from the start of a sentence.
when: The name is a generic drug or chemical name rather than a proprietary name.
The word is a former brand name that has become a common generic term, or has a distinct generic meaning.
Ordinary sentence-initial capitalisation is an exception.
rules.why: G-2 consolidates the same inappropriate-capital finding for generic chemicals and genericised brand words; E-1 preserves both branded and distinct generic senses as correct.

covers.quote: ‘Trade mark’ is spelled as 2 words in the Trade Marks Act 1995.
You should also spell ‘trade mark’ as 2 words when you use it as a verb

rules.quote: Use this spelling when writing for government, even though most dictionaries prefer ‘trademark’.
rules.violation_condition: The term ‘trade mark’ is written as one word or as a hyphenated word rather than as 2 words, including when used as a verb.
when: Applies to government writing.
The 2-word spelling applies to both noun and verb uses.
rules.why: G-2 makes noun and verb uses conditions of one spelling check; the separate preference for ‘register’ changes wording rather than spelling.

parts.quote: Register your brand as a trade mark if you don’t want others to use it.

rules.quote: it’s better to say ‘register a trade mark’.
rules.violation_condition: ‘Trade mark’ is used as a verb to describe registration instead of a construction using ‘register’.
when: The intended meaning is registering a trade mark.
This is a preference over verbal ‘trade mark’, not a declaration that the alternative is incorrect English.
rules.why: The preferred verb construction creates a different finding from the 2-word spelling check; E-1 prevents relabelling the manual's other correct example as incorrect.

covers.quote: Avoid using trade marks and brand names if possible. Instead use a generic word.

rules.quote: Use a common word for a product if you can
rules.specification: Interpret ‘if you can’ as applying when substitution preserves the intended meaning. A brand needed to identify a particular product or business is outside this preference.
rules.violation_condition: A trade mark or brand name is used to identify a kind of product when an equivalent generic word would convey the intended meaning.
when: A suitable generic term is available.
The intended meaning does not require identification of the particular brand.
rules.why: G-4 treats the heading and body as one preference; G-2 retains the feasibility condition rather than creating a blanket ban on brand names.

covers.quote: The trade mark symbol can be used with registered and unregistered trade marks.
Businesses can use it when they intend to register the term or when registration is pending.

rules.quote: Avoid using the registered (®) symbol or the trade mark (™) symbol for trade marks if possible.
rules.specification: The page does not define when inclusion of a symbol is unavoidable. Applicability needs a decision about whether the symbol can be omitted; merely discussing a symbol is not displaying it for a trade mark.
rules.violation_condition: An avoidable ® or ™ symbol is included with a trade mark.
when: The symbol is used to label a trade mark.
Omitting the symbol is possible.
This preference does not make ™ legally unavailable for unregistered marks: it can accompany registered or unregistered marks, including intended or pending registrations.
rules.why: G-2 keeps avoidance of both symbols in one check; G-3 records permissions without turning them into requirements or automatic exemptions from the preference.

covers.quote: The registered symbol shows a trade mark is registered.

rules.quote: It’s illegal to use it if the trade mark is not registered.
rules.violation_condition: The registered symbol ® is used for a trade mark that is not registered in the relevant jurisdiction.
when: ® is being used as a registered-trade-mark symbol.
Registration status is assessed for the relevant country.
This registration restriction does not apply to ™.
rules.why: The stated illegality supports MUST_NOT; false registration marking is a different reason for a finding from the general preference to omit symbols.

covers.quote: This may vary between different countries.
A few words have different meanings when used as a trade mark or used generically.

examples.note: A distinct generic meaning, not another brand of sticking plaster.

rules.quote: If a term is still registered as a trade mark, you should use it only for that brand
rules.violation_condition: A currently registered trade mark is used as a generic product name or to identify a product from another brand rather than the registered brand.
when: The term remains registered as a trade mark in the relevant country.
The term is being used to name a product or brand.
Distinct generic meanings presented by the manual, such as ‘bandaid’ for a makeshift solution and ‘google’ as a search verb, are not references to the registered product.
rules.why: The brand-reference restriction is a semantic check separate from capitalisation; G-2 retains jurisdiction and meaning conditions, and E-1 keeps both correct senses compliant.
